title: Finding Elements with Playwright Locators
excerpt: Before Playwright can click a button, enter text, or check something on a webpage, it needs to find the element first. In this part, we'll learn the most useful Playwright locators and practice choosing the right one for real-world situations.
html:
What is a Locator?

In the previous article, we installed Playwright and created our first test.

Now let's look at something you'll use in almost every Playwright test: locators.

Suppose you're testing a login page. You want Playwright to enter an email address into the email field. But how does Playwright know which field you're talking about?

You need to tell it. That's what a locator does.

A locator tells Playwright:

"Find this particular element on the page."

Once Playwright finds the element, we can perform actions on it.

Step 1: Create the Test File

Inside your project's tests folder, create:

tests/locators.spec.ts

Add the following code:

import { test } from "@playwright/test";

test("Practice Playwright locators", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");
});

We're using the SauceDemo login page throughout this article.

Open the page in your browser and take a moment to look at the login form.

You should see:

We'll use these elements to practice our locators.

Step 2: getByRole()

getByRole() finds an element based on its role, such as a button, link, heading, checkbox, or textbox.

For example, the Login button on SauceDemo is:

<input type="submit" value="Login">

Even though it's an <input> element in the HTML, Playwright understands that it behaves as a button.

So we can find it using:

const loginButton = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

This is much easier to understand than trying to find the element using its CSS class or ID.

Why is getByRole() recommended?

Because it describes the element from a user's perspective.

We're telling Playwright:

Find the button named Login.

rather than:

Find the element with this particular class.

This usually makes our tests easier to read and maintain.

Step 3: getByLabel()

getByLabel() is especially useful for form fields.

However, there's an important detail with our SauceDemo login form.

The Username and Password inputs don't have associated <label> elements. They only have placeholder text:

<input placeholder="Username" ...>

<input placeholder="Password" ...>

So getByLabel() would not be the right locator for these particular fields.

That's actually useful to understand.

A locator isn't something we choose just because we know its name. We choose it based on the actual HTML of the page.

For a page that has:

<label>Email</label>
<input ...>

we could use:

const emailInput = page.getByLabel("Email");

So remember:

Use getByLabel() when the form field has a proper accessible label.

Step 4: getByPlaceholder()

Our SauceDemo login form gives us a perfect example of getByPlaceholder().

The Username field has:

placeholder="Username"

So we can locate it with:

const usernameInput = page.getByPlaceholder("Username");

And the Password field:

const passwordInput = page.getByPlaceholder("Password");

This is easy to read:

page.getByPlaceholder("Username");

means:

Find the input whose placeholder says "Username".

For this particular page, this is a perfectly reasonable locator.

Step 5: getByTestId()

Now let's look at another useful option.

SauceDemo provides test-specific attributes:

data-test="username"
data-test="password"
data-test="login-button"

Playwright can use these through getByTestId().

For example:

const usernameInput = page.getByTestId("username");

const passwordInput = page.getByTestId("password");

const loginButton = page.getByTestId("login-button");

This is a good example of why test IDs can be useful.

The developers have provided identifiers specifically for these elements.

If the CSS class changes from:

form_input

to something completely different, our test can still work as long as the test ID stays the same.

Step 6: getByText()

getByText() finds an element based on the visible text on the page.

For example, imagine the application displays an error message:

Epic sadface: Username is required

We could locate it using:

const errorMessage = page.getByText("Epic sadface: Username is required");

This is useful when you need to find a message, heading, or other visible text.

However, don't automatically use getByText() for everything.

If you're looking for a button, getByRole() is usually a better choice.

For example:

page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

is preferable to:

page.getByText("Login");

because we're specifically looking for a button.

Step 7: getByAltText()

getByAltText() is used to find images through their alt attribute.

For example, if a page contains:

<img src="logo.png" alt="Company Logo">

you can use:

const logo = page.getByAltText("Company Logo");

This isn't useful for our SauceDemo login inputs, because they aren't images.

That's an important point:

Not every locator is suitable for every element.

Choose the locator based on the HTML and purpose of the element.

Step 8: getByTitle()

getByTitle() finds an element using its title attribute.

For example:

<button title="Search">
  Search
</button>

You could locate it with:

const searchButton = page.getByTitle("Search");

Again, this isn't something we need for the SauceDemo login page because these elements don't have a useful title attribute.

You'll see this locator less often than getByRole(), getByLabel(), or getByTestId().

Choosing the Right Locator

Let's look at our SauceDemo login page again.

We have:

<input
  placeholder="Username"
  data-test="username"
  id="user-name"
>

There are several ways we could find this element.

For example:

page.getByPlaceholder("Username");

or:

page.getByTestId("username");

Both can work. So which one should we use?

There isn't always one single answer.

A good approach is to prefer a locator that is:

  • Easy to understand

  • Stable

  • Closely related to how the user interacts with the page

For the Login button, I'd prefer:

page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

For the Username field on this particular page:

page.getByTestId("username");

or:

page.getByPlaceholder("Username");

Both are reasonable choices.

A Small Real-World Example

Now let's put a few of these locators together.

Replace your locators.spec.ts content with:

import { test } from "@playwright/test";

test("Find elements on the SauceDemo login page", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");

  const usernameInput = page.getByTestId("username");
  const passwordInput = page.getByTestId("password");
  const loginButton = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

  console.log(usernameInput);
  console.log(passwordInput);
  console.log(loginButton);
});

We aren't clicking or typing anything yet.

We're simply telling Playwright:

Find these three elements for me.

Practice

Now create another file:

tests/locator-practice.spec.ts

Use the SauceDemo login page and create locators for these three elements:

  1. Username using getByPlaceholder()

  2. Password using getByTestId()

  3. Login button using getByRole()

Try writing them yourself first.

Your final locators should look similar to:

const usernameInput = page.getByPlaceholder("Username");

const passwordInput = page.getByTestId("password");

const loginButton = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

Don't perform any actions yet. The goal of this exercise is simply to become comfortable finding elements.

One Important Habit: Inspect the DOM

When you're working with a real application, don't guess your locators.

Open the browser's Developer Tools, inspect the element, and look at its HTML.

For our SauceDemo Username field, we can see:

<input
  class="input_error form_input"
  placeholder="Username"
  type="text"
  data-test="username"
  id="user-name"
  name="user-name"
>

Now we have enough information to choose a locator.

We can see the placeholder:

Username

and the test ID:

username

That's much better than randomly trying selectors until something works.

As you continue learning Playwright, inspecting the DOM and choosing a stable locator should become a normal part of your workflow.

A Simple End-to-End Login Test

So far, we've focused on finding elements with Playwright locators.

Before moving to the next topic, let's use those locators in a small real-world example. We'll log in to SauceDemo and verify that the login was successful.

We haven't covered Playwright actions in detail yet, so don't worry about memorizing these methods. We'll learn them properly later.

Step 1: Create the Test File

Inside the tests folder, create:

tests/login.spec.ts

Add this code:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("User can log in successfully", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");

  await page.getByTestId("username").fill("standard_user");
  await page.getByTestId("password").fill("secret_sauce");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" }).click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/inventory/);
});

Step 2: What Did We Just Do?

Our test performs a complete login flow:

Open SauceDemo
      ↓
Enter username
      ↓
Enter password
      ↓
Click Login
      ↓
Verify the inventory page

Let's quickly look at the two new methods we haven't covered yet.

.fill()

await page.getByTestId("username").fill("standard_user");

.fill() puts text into an input field.

Here, Playwright finds the Username field and enters:

standard_user

The same thing happens with the Password field:

await page.getByTestId("password").fill("secret_sauce");

.click()

await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" }).click();

.click() clicks an element.

Here, Playwright finds the Login button and clicks it.

That's all you need to know about .fill() and .click() for now. We'll cover Playwright actions properly later in the series.

Step 3: Verify the Login

After clicking Login, SauceDemo takes the user to the inventory page.

We verify that using:

await expect(page).toHaveURL(/inventory/);

toHaveURL() checks the current browser URL.

Here, /inventory/ means we are checking whether the URL contains the word inventory.

If the login is successful, the assertion passes.

Step 4: Run the Test

Open your terminal inside the Playwright project and run:

npx playwright test tests/login.spec.ts

This tells Playwright to run only the login.spec.ts file.

If you want to watch the browser while the test runs, use:

npx playwright test tests/login.spec.ts --project=chromium --headed

This means:

  • tests/login.spec.ts → Run this specific test file

  • --project=chromium → Run it using Chromium

  • --headed → Show the browser while the test is running

You should see the browser open, enter the username and password, click Login, and navigate to the inventory page.

Practice

Make one small change to the test.

After the login, instead of checking the URL, try verifying that the inventory page contains the heading:

Products

You'll need to use a Playwright locator and an assertion.

Try it yourself before looking at the solution.

We'll learn assertions in more detail later, so for now focus on understanding how locators + actions + assertions work together to create a complete test.

Practice Solution

For the practice, we want to verify that the inventory page contains the Products heading after login.

Here's the complete solution:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("User can log in successfully", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");

  await page.getByTestId("username").fill("standard_user");
  await page.getByTestId("password").fill("secret_sauce");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText("Products")).toBeVisible();
});

What changed?

Instead of checking the URL:

await expect(page).toHaveURL(/inventory/);

we now check whether the Products text is visible:

await expect(page.getByText("Products")).toBeVisible();

Here:

  • getByText("Products") finds the element containing Products.

  • toBeVisible() checks that the element is actually visible on the page.

So our test now verifies something the user can actually see after logging in.
